newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Verdicts in Bosnia shooting trial "mockery" - Bildt.
newsitem.headline: Verdicts in Bosnia shooting trial "mockery" - Bildt.

text.p: The top international official in Bosnia on Friday branded the outcome of the trial in a Bosnian Croat court of Croat policemen in connection with the killing and wounding of Moslem pilgrims in Mostar "a complete mockery and farce."

Five Bosnian Croat policemen were tried in Croat-held Mostar on Thursday for their involvement in a February 10 incident in which one Moslem was killed and 21 wounded while trying to visit a Moslem cemetery in a Croat sector of the ethnically divided town.

After a brief trial, the court found three policemen guilty of criminal mistreatment and overstepping their authority and handed down suspended sentences of six months to one year's jail. Two other policemen were acquitted.

"I spoke to Carl Bildt this morning and his exact words were 'a complete mockery and farce'," said Colum Murphy, spokesman for Bildt, the international High Representative in Bosnia, describing Bildt's reaction to the verdict.

A United Nations report, based on photographs taken of the incident, identified three Croat policemen, including a deputy police chief, as firing into the crowd of 200 Moslem civilians on February 10, and two officers as having their weapons drawn during the shooting.
The shootings stirred an international outcry and calls for the immediate dismissal and criminal prosecution of the perpetrators.

U.N. police spokesman Alex Ivanko said the five policemen had been charged not with killing and wounding civilians, but for "going beyond their duties when using physical force and rubber truncheons".
"During this court's hearing, probably one of the speediest known to man, only the defendants and other west Mostar police officers were questioned," Ivanko said.
"No testimonies were taken from the victims or witnesses," and the court had taken only 45 minutes to reach a verdict, he added.

One of the policemen found guilty was sentenced to a year and the other two to six months in prison, but all the sentences were suspended. The court said it must not be forgotten that the police officers were defending their country.
"This verdict is disappointing and deeply troubling, although not suprising to those who have been following the latest developments in West Mostar," said Ivanko.

Hardline Croats declared a mini-state in the Herzegovina region during the 3-1/2 year war in Bosnia and have resisted international pressure to merge it with the Moslem-Croat federation formed under U.S. pressure in 1994.
Ivanko said the court had no understanding of professional police responsibilities and was still entrenched in war-time rhetoric.
"The (Croat) criminal justice system requires total and urgent reform to correspond with what is expected in a democratic society," he said.
